readme.title: What this module covers
readme.html:
What this module covers

This module lays the groundwork for the course, starting from the client-server model and the coffee shop analogy used throughout. It defines cloud computing, compares cloud-based, on-premises and hybrid deployments, and lists the six benefits of the AWS Cloud. It then introduces AWS Regions and Availability Zones as the basis for high availability and fault tolerance, and explains how the AWS Shared Responsibility Model divides security work. A closing real-life case shows how these ideas combine for a company expanding worldwide.

readme.title: Lessons
readme.html:
Lessons

Only the six content lessons have notes files: the course's opening "How to Use Each Module" lesson covers the course player, not AWS, and the Assessment and Module Summary feed this page.

Module 1 Introduction

  1. Welcome to AWS Cloud Practitioner Essentials: the client-server model through the coffee shop, where cloud computing fits in it, and why you pay only for what you use.

The AWS Cloud

  1. What is Cloud Computing?: how AWS started, the four-part definition of cloud computing, data centers, and the cloud-based, on-premises and hybrid deployment types.
  2. Benefits of the AWS Cloud: the six benefits, from trading fixed for variable expense to going global in minutes.
  3. Introduction to AWS Global Infrastructure: Regions, Availability Zones, and how they deliver high availability and fault tolerance.
  4. The AWS Shared Responsibility Model: security of the cloud versus security in the cloud, plus the duties that vary by service.

Cloud in Real Life

  1. Applying Cloud Concepts to Real Life Use Cases: a Seattle ecommerce company uses Regions, AZs and the shared responsibility split to expand to Ireland and Singapore.

readme.title: Key takeaways
readme.html:
Key takeaways

  • A client requests, and a server validates, processes and replies, and cloud computing is a version of this client-server model that supplies scalable servers over the internet.
  • The course defines cloud computing in four parts, in order: (1) on-demand delivery (2) of IT resources (3) over the internet (4) with pay-as-you-go pricing.
  • Resources can be provisioned when needed and deprovisioned when not, and billing stops right away.
  • The three deployment types are cloud-based, on-premises and hybrid, and hybrid fits when some systems must stay in-house.
  • The six benefits of the AWS Cloud are trade fixed expense for variable expense, benefit from massive economies of scale, stop guessing capacity, increase speed and agility, stop spending money running and maintaining data centers, and go global in minutes.
  • A Region holds three or more Availability Zones, and each Availability Zone is an isolated part of one Region that houses one or more data centers.
  • Spreading resources across multiple AZs, and across Regions for disaster protection, gives high availability and fault tolerance.
  • AWS handles security of the cloud, including all physical data center security, while customers handle security in the cloud, including their OS patches, applications, data and client-side encryption.
  • Some duties, such as server-side encryption and firewall configuration, shift between AWS and the customer depending on the service.

readme.title: Summary
readme.html:
Summary

The module builds one picture in layers. The cloud is the client-server model offered as on-demand, internet-reached, pay-as-you-go resources, and that model is where the six business benefits come from. AWS Global Infrastructure, with Regions made of Availability Zones made of data centers, is what lets those resources stay highly available and fault tolerant around the world. The AWS Shared Responsibility Model then draws the security line: AWS protects that infrastructure, and customers protect what they build on it. The ecommerce case shows all of these at work in a single design.

welcome-to-aws-cloud-practitioner-essent.html:
Welcome to AWS Cloud Practitioner Essentials

Objectives

  • Explain in simple terms how a and a work together.

Notes

Where the course starts

  • The first section covers what the cloud is, what it does for a business, and how AWS and customers divide security work.
  • Instructors Morgan Willis, Rudy Chetty and Alan Meridian teach with analogies, use cases and service demos, starting simple.
  • AWS offers storage, databases, compute, content delivery, and much more, but the course opens with one basic idea.

The client-server model

  • A client asks for something, and a server does the work and sends back the result.
  • In the coffee shop, the customer is the client and the barista is the server, which on AWS would be a .
  • One exchange has three steps:
    1. Request: the client asks, here for a coffee, though a request can be for any data or analysis a business needs.
    2. Validation: the server checks the request is legitimate and allowed, as a barista checks payment and the menu.
    3. Response: the server hands back the result, a finished drink.
  • The client depends on the server to fulfil requests, and the server does nothing until a client asks.
  • Real applications involve many requests and servers, which the course builds up to.

Where cloud computing fits

  • The cloud does not replace the , which modern applications still use.
  • is one version of it, supplying the server side as scalable servers that clients reach over the internet.
  • A server usually both stores and processes data, while the client sends requests and shows the replies, and cloud servers scale for both kinds of demand.

Coffee shop connections

  • Later lessons keep mapping shop elements to cloud functions, such as AWS compute instance types to coffee machines each suited to a kind of work.
  • The analogy exists to make abstract cloud ideas concrete.

Paying only for what you use

  • You pay only for the AWS resources you consume, just as staff earn wages only for hours on shift.
  • A shop owner adds staff on busy days and cuts back on slow ones.
    • Example: ten baristas on all day for a new drink launch cover the rush but sit idle, still paid, in quiet hours.
  • An on-premises is just as rigid, because its capacity cannot be multiplied at short notice.
  • On AWS there is no prepayment, and you need not worry about capacity constraints.
  • You provision resources when demand appears and deprovision them as fast when it fades, by hand or automatically through configuration.
  • Billing for a resource ends the moment it is deprovisioned.

Visuals

  • The AWS Cloud Practitioner Coffee Shop graphic: four markers, one on how shop elements will stand in for cloud functions and three introducing the instructors.

Key takeaways

  • A client-server exchange runs request, validation, processing and response, with the client relying on the server for the work.
  • Cloud computing is a form of the client-server model that provides scalable servers over the internet, and on AWS the server is a virtual server.
  • AWS charges only for what you consume, with nothing paid upfront.
  • Provision resources when demand rises and deprovision them when it falls, and charges stop as soon as a resource is gone.

Scenarios

  • A customer orders a coffee and the barista checks the order before serving it: the client-server model.
  • Ten baristas paid all day for a launch, some of them idle: fixed capacity, which paying only for use avoids.

Terms

  • Client: the side that sends requests and displays the responses.
  • Server: the side that validates requests, stores and processes data, and returns responses.
  • Client-server model: clients send requests and servers process them and reply, and cloud computing is one form of it.
  • Virtual server: a server you use on AWS over the internet, in AWS data centers rather than your own.
  • Provisioning: setting up resources when you need them.
  • Deprovisioning: releasing unneeded resources, which ends their charges immediately.
  • Coffee shop analogy: the course's running metaphor mapping coffee shop parts to cloud concepts.

what-is-cloud-computing.html:
What is Cloud Computing?

Objectives

  • State what means.
  • Compare the deployment types.

Notes

From Amazon.com to AWS

  • Amazon.com, then selling books and other goods, kept scaling its servers, and in 2003 planned to rent such resources out on demand, which could spare others upfront hardware costs.
  • (November 2004) was the first public infrastructure service, with and two years later.
  • Start-ups and developers came first, then enterprises drawn by scalability, cost and ease of use, and with databases, networking and analytics added, AWS now powers much of the internet as a global leader.

The definition, part by part

  • : resources in seconds, scaled up or down without long setup, the idea AWS began with.
  • IT resources: servers, storage, databases, networking, AI/ML tools and more, to build and run applications.
  • Over the internet: remote use through web-based services, not local hardware, from anywhere.
  • : pay for consumption, not fixed long-term contracts, for cost efficiency and flexibility.

Data centers

  • A is one or more buildings of servers with redundant power, cooling and security.
  • Firms once ran their own or co-located, but AWS lets them use data centers they do not own, trading upkeep and repetitive chores for innovation.

Cloud deployment types

  • Cloud-based (public cloud): all in the cloud, migrated or newly built, for example moving data first, then building an app of virtual servers, databases and networking.
    • It scales well with little upfront cost, but alone cannot keep sensitive data on premises for compliance.
  • On-premises: largely legacy IT plus virtualization and application management to try to lift utilization, missing many cloud benefits but offering dedicated resources and low latency.
  • Hybrid: in-house and cloud resources together, for legacy systems kept in-house for maintenance or regulation.
    • Multi-cloud setups can also count as hybrid.
  • Compliance shapes the choice but is not a deployment type.

Visuals

  • Definition graphic: one marker per part of the definition.
  • Deployment flashcards: one card per deployment type.

Key takeaways

  • Definition, in order: (1) on-demand delivery (2) of IT resources (3) over the internet (4) with pay-as-you-go pricing.
  • Deleting or deprovisioning a resource stops its charges at once.
  • Cloud-based is all cloud and on-premises all in-house, while hybrid mixes them when some systems must stay on premises.

Scenarios

  • 2,000 TB in Amazon S3, deleted when unneeded: on-demand delivery and pay-as-you-go pricing.
  • Regulated legacy apps on site, advanced analytics in the cloud: .

Terms

  • Cloud computing: IT resources, on demand, over the internet, billed pay-as-you-go.
  • On-demand delivery: resources within seconds, whenever needed.
  • Pay-as-you-go pricing: paying only for what you consume.
  • Data center: a server building with redundant power, cooling and security.
  • Co-location: hosting in a shared facility.
  • Amazon Simple Queue Service: the first public AWS infrastructure service.
  • Amazon S3: the AWS data storage service.
  • Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud: the AWS scalable compute service.
  • Cloud-based deployment: everything in the cloud, also called public cloud.
  • On-premises deployment: in-house resources, close to legacy IT.
  • Hybrid deployment: in-house plus cloud resources.
  • Multi-cloud deployment: left undefined, only said to count as hybrid.

benefits-of-the-aws-cloud.html:
Benefits of the AWS Cloud

Objectives

  • Recognize the six cloud benefits and match a business problem to the right one.

Notes

Trade fixed expense for variable expense

  • Owning a means paying hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars upfront for space, hardware, staff and upkeep, then budgeting around it even when usage is low.
  • On AWS the bill follows monthly usage, so you start small, spending matches consumption for more financial flexibility, and billing and budgeting tools help you save.
  • The course sometimes says upfront expense instead of .
  • Exam guide update verified 2026-10-09, Six advantages of cloud computing Fixed costs are paid up front for data centers and servers whether or not you use them, while variable costs on AWS follow only what you actually consume.

Benefit from massive economies of scale

  • AWS buys hardware in bulk for its worldwide data centers and passes the lower prices on.
  • So startups, not only big enterprises, can afford advanced technology.

Stop guessing capacity

  • On premises you buy hardware for a forecast: plan for 10 million users over three years and get about 500,000, and the excess sits idle, while underestimating means a scramble for servers, degraded service and lost customers.
  • On AWS you provision for today and scale with real demand in minutes, not weeks or months, keeping performance optimal without over- or under-provisioning.

Increase speed and agility

  • Teams spin up test environments, try ideas and delete failures so costs stop, shifting time from provisioning and deprovisioning to innovating and optimizing.
  • Faster deployment shortens time to market and quickens responses to change.

Stop spending money running and maintaining data centers

  • A data center keeps costing money after it is built, for utilities, maintenance, and racking, stacking and powering servers.
  • AWS runs that physical layer, freeing time and money for customers and strategy.
  • The timeline words this benefit with "to run and maintain" instead.

Go global in minutes

  • A US company expanding to India can deploy to an AWS-managed Region there instead of building its own data centers, in minutes rather than months or years.
  • Exam guide update verified 2026-10-09, Six advantages of cloud computing The exam guide calls this benefit speed of deployment: with go global in minutes, you deploy an application to multiple Regions around the world with just a few clicks.

Visuals

  • Six benefits timeline: one explained step per benefit.

Key takeaways

  • The six benefits by their course names: trade fixed expense for , benefit from massive , stop guessing capacity, increase speed and agility, stop spending money running and maintaining data centers, and go global in minutes.
  • Together they save money and time and open up AWS's worldwide footprint.
  • On AWS, spending follows usage and capacity follows demand.

Scenarios

  • Hardware for 10 million users, about 500,000 arrive: stop guessing capacity.
  • Throwaway test environments for new ideas: increase speed and agility.
  • A US company deploying to a Region in India: go global in minutes.

Terms

  • Fixed expense: a cost that does not change with usage.
  • Variable expense: a cost that follows consumption, like an AWS bill.
  • Economies of scale: lower unit prices from huge purchase volumes.
  • Scaling: adjusting resources up or down to demand.

introduction-to-aws-global-infrastructur.html:
Introduction to AWS Global Infrastructure

Objectives

  • Describe how Regions, Availability Zones and data centers nest.
  • Explain what and give a business.

Notes

Global reach buys availability

  • Beyond going global in minutes, global reach brings high availability.
  • Coffee shop version: a mishap closes one branch, but the chain's nearby branches keep serving.
  • One giant is the opposite, since one outage or disaster stops every application.
  • High availability: minimal downtime, because a standby takes over when one component fails.
  • Fault tolerance: going further, the system runs on when several components fail, via resilience in every layer.

Region, Availability Zone, data center

Level Key facts
Region Geographic area near customers (such as Ohio, Dublin, Tokyo, Paris, Sao Paulo), sited partly for availability, with three or more physically separate AZs
Isolated location in one Region (never spanning Regions) with its own power, networking and connectivity, kept apart from other AZs as a disaster could cut off a whole AZ
Data center One or more per AZ, with redundant power, networking and connectivity
  • Nearby users get low-latency, fault-tolerant access to services, and advanced components come later.

Designing for availability

  • Spread resources and replicate data across several AZs so one AZ's outage does not stop applications.
  • For disaster protection, businesses often run in several Regions with .
  • High availability means business resources stay up, which no single storage location or data center ensures.

Visuals

  • Regions and AZs graphic: a Region containing three AZs, one marker per level.

Key takeaways

  • A Region holds three or more AZs, and each AZ is an isolated part of one Region holding one or more data centers.
  • High availability limits downtime from one failure, fault tolerance survives several, and both come from spreading resources across AZs and Regions.
  • Never rely on one data center, however secure.

Scenarios

  • One coffee chain branch closes, others serve: high availability.
  • A Region outage triggers failover to another Region: multi-Region deployment.

Terms

  • AWS Global Infrastructure: AWS's Regions, AZs and data centers worldwide.
  • AWS Region: a geographic area with three or more AZs.
  • Availability Zone (AZ): an isolated location in a Region, with one or more data centers.
  • High availability: minimal downtime via standby components.
  • Fault tolerance: operating on despite multiple failures.
  • Failover: switching to another AZ or Region when one fails.

the-aws-shared-responsibility-model.html:
The AWS Shared Responsibility Model

Objectives

  • Sort security duties into AWS, customer and shared.
  • Name the model's components.

Notes

Who secures what

  • House analogy: the builder makes the doors solid, the owner locks them.
Owner Duties
AWS (of the cloud) Upkeep of facilities, hardware, networking and software behind all services; physical security, never shared (door locks, access control lists, privilege separation, surveillance, environmental controls); network and isolation of customers
Customer (in the cloud) The OS you run (as in the video) and its patches, applications, data, access,
Varies by service , traffic protection, platform and application management, OS, network and firewall configuration
  • Only you can sign in to your OS or add users, since AWS has no back door.
  • The vendor supplies OS patches, but applying them is yours alone.
  • You choose what data to store and, via AWS controls, who reaches it: everyone, some users, one person under conditions, or nobody.
  • Encrypted data stays unreadable even if access is left open.

Visuals

  • Components graphic: three markers, for customer, shared and AWS duties.

Key takeaways

  • AWS owns , including all physical security, and the customer owns .
  • Customers patch their OS and secure applications, data, access and client-side encryption.
  • Server-side encryption and OS, network and firewall setup vary by service.

Scenarios

  • AWS spots a flaw in a customer's OS: it can only alert them, and they patch.
  • Public retail photos versus locked-down bank records: customer-controlled access.

Terms

  • AWS Shared Responsibility Model: AWS and customers dividing security for an environment both can trust.
  • Security of the cloud: AWS's share.
  • Security in the cloud: the customer's share.
  • Hypervisor layer: a virtualization layer that AWS secures.
  • Client-side encryption: encrypting data on the client before the server gets it.
  • Server-side encryption: encryption by the service, owner varying by service.

applying-cloud-concepts-to-real-life-use.html:
Applying Cloud Concepts to Real Life Use Cases

Objectives

  • Follow one company's expansion to see Regions, AZs and the working side by side.

Notes

Cloud in Real Life segments

  • These recurring segments apply the deliberately simplified course concepts to realistic business problems, showing services combining like building blocks.

Going global: Regions and Availability Zones

  • The company, based in Seattle, Washington, wants customers worldwide, but the farther its servers are from them the higher the .
  • It therefore hosts its application in Regions close to its main customer groups:
    • Europe: in Ireland.
    • Asia: Singapore, (remember the video's code, as the graphic's ap-southwest-1 conflicts with it).
  • Each extra Region raises availability, and in Ireland it runs the same configuration in two AZs and fails over if one breaks, which the course calls designing for and .
  • Existing Regions let it reach new markets in minutes, not the months or years of building sites, and without big upfront capital, which especially helps startups.

Shared responsibility in the same design

  • AWS secures the Ireland and all physical infrastructure, so the company never picks data center door locks.
  • The company's own focus is higher-level: encrypting and protecting its data, controlling access to its AWS resources, and setting up applications to comply with card-payment rules.
  • This is versus in practice.

Visuals

  • Ecommerce expansion graphic: three markers tracing the company from Seattle to Ireland and Singapore, with Region choice, availability gains and the security split.

Key takeaways

  • Global infrastructure and shared responsibility work together in a real design, not as separate topics.
  • Hosting in Regions near customers cuts latency.
  • Several Regions plus at least two AZs with failover deliver high availability and fault tolerance.
  • With physical security handled by AWS, the company focuses on data, access and compliant configuration.

Scenarios

  • Serving Europe from eu-west-1: picking Regions to cut latency.
  • Opening in Singapore within minutes: go global in minutes.
  • Mirroring the setup across two AZs: high availability and fault tolerance.
  • The company encrypts its data while AWS guards the buildings: the AWS Shared Responsibility Model.

Terms

  • Cloud in Real Life: a recurring segment applying concepts to realistic cases.
  • Latency: delay in answering requests, growing with distance from the infrastructure.
  • eu-west-1: the Ireland Region code in this example.
  • ap-southeast-1: the Singapore Region code given in the video.

options.text: AWS guarding the buildings that hold its storage

options.text: Client-side encryption

options.text: Encryption at rest

options.text: Customers in Singapore

options.text: Customers in the United Kingdom

options.text: Serve the site from a Region much closer to its main users
options.why: Answers travel a shorter distance when the site runs near its users, so each response arrives sooner.

options.why: A second Availability Zone helps the site survive a failure, but it sits just as far from Europe as before.

read.text: Latency: delay in answering requests, growing with distance from the infrastructure.

options.text: The share of time an application stays reachable for users
options.why: That describes availability, which more Regions and Availability Zones improve, not the delay itself.

cards.text: The cafe skips a big server purchase and pays each month for what the order app actually used
In the quiet winter months the computing bill shrinks along with the orders
A tiny cafe startup can afford the same advanced technology as a national chain
